subdivision.heading: Additional Rules Specific to Originating Applications for Judicial Review

operative_text.controlling:
3.24(1)  If an originating applicant is entitled to a declaration that a
decision or act of a person or body is unauthorized or invalid, the
Court may, instead of making a declaration, set aside the decision
or act.
(2)  The Court may
(a) direct a person or body to reconsider the whole or any part
of a matter,
(b) direct a person or body to reconsider the whole or any part
of a decision if the Court has set aside the decision under
subrule (1), and
(c) give any other directions it considers necessary.
(3)  If the sole ground for a remedy is a defect in form or a
technical irregularity, the Court may, if the Court finds that no
substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice has occurred, despite
the defect,
(a) refuse a remedy, or
(b) validate the decision made to have effect from a date and
subject to any terms and conditions that the Court
considers appropriate.

BOOK_B.title: Additional remedies on judicial review
BOOK_B.operative_text_raw: (1) If an originating applicant is entitled to a declaration that a decision or act of a person or body is unauthorized or invalid, the Court may, instead of making a declaration, set aside the decision or act. (2) The Court may (a) direct a person or body to reconsider the whole or any part of a matter, (b) direct a person or body to reconsider the whole or any part of a decision if the Court has set aside the decision under subrule (1), and (c) give any other directions it considers necessary. (3) If the sole ground for a remedy is a defect in form or a technical irregularity, the Court may, if the Court finds that no substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice has occurred, despite the defect, (a) refuse a remedy, or (b) validate the decision made to have effect from a date and subject to any terms and conditions that the Court considers appropriate. 1. Overview of Court's Discretion In Morawetz v. Alberta (Director of SafeRoads), 2024 ABKB 588, Justice Marion discussed the Court's discretion to direct an administrative tribunal to reconsider its decision. His Lordship said: [30] Rules 3.24(2)(a) and (b) provide the Court a wide discretion to direct an administrative tribunal to reconsider a whole or part of a matter, or to reconsider whole or part of a decision where the Court quashes the decision. Rule 3.24(c) provides the Court jurisdiction to give any other direction it considers necessary in addition to remitting the matter back to the tribunal for reconsideration: Penn v St Stephen's College, 2024 ABCA 99 at para 65. [31] The Court's findings and directions must be considered by and are binding on the tribunal (unless the law changes subsequent to the directions): Régie des rentes du Québec v Canada Bread Company Ltd, 2013 SCC 46 at para 46; Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v Yansane, 2017 FCA 48 at paras 19, 23, 25; Mohammed v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2022 FC 980 at para 44. [32] The discretion to provide directions to an administrative tribunal is part of the multi-faceted question of the appropriate remedy that engages consideration of the Court's common law and statutory jurisdiction and the “great diversity of elements that may influence” the Court's decision in respect of available remedies: Vavilov at para 139. [33] For example, courts outside the SafeRoads context have confirmed the discretion to direct that a reconsideration: (a) be conducted by a different person or panel: United Nurses of Alberta v Alberta Health Services, 2021 ABCA 194 at para 102. There is no fixed rule but, factors considered include fairness and the appearance of impartiality, practicality, and efficiency, the proper administration of justice, cost-efficient decision making and access to justice: United Nurses at paras 103-104; Edmonton Police Service v Furlong, 2013 ABCA 177 at para 3; Vavilov at paras 139-140; (b) be bound by the previous findings of the tribunal: Shuchuk v Alberta (Workers' Compensation Board), 2012 ABCA 50 at para 43 [Shuchuk 2012]. In Sharif v Canada (Attorney General), 2018 FCA 205, at para 54, the Court implied that the tribunal would be bound by its earlier factual findings when the Court decided not to remit the matter due to the inevitable result based on those findings; (c) be limited to specific issues, excluding specific issues, or directing that specifically identified issues must be addressed: Shuchuk 2012 at para 43; Shell Canada Limited v Alberta (Energy), 2023 ABCA 230 at para 59; Yatar v TD Insurance Meloche Monnex, 2024 SCC 8 at para 77; Shuchuk v Alberta (Workers' Compensation Board), 2007 ABCA 213 at para 50; Clark v City of Medicine Hat, 2024 ABKB 513 at paras 71-72; Hannora (Re), 2020 ONCA 161 at para 3; Dr Mays Abdulghafoor v University of Calgary, 2021 ABQB 187 at para 124; Pincher Creek (Town of) v Municipal Government Board, 2006 ABQB 513 at para 18; Shields v Information and Privacy Commissioner, 2004 ABQB 353 at para 74; Schroder v Alberta (Workers' Compensation Board), 2009 ABQB 583 at para 22; Thornhill v Superintendent of Motor Vehicles, 2016 BCSC 1202 at paras 30-31[1]; Kessler v British Columbia (Superintendent of Motor Vehicles), 2017 BCSC 809 at para 20; David Burr Ltd v Zahm, 2012 BCSC 897 at paras 10-13; (d) be based on the original record, or permitting or directing a different or augmented record: Chartrand v Alberta (Human Rights and Citizenship Commission), 2008 ABQB 207 at para 28; Hamilton v Alberta (Labour Relations Board), 1993 CanLII 7143 (AB KB) at para 32; Garnett v British Columbia (Superintendent of Motor Vehicles), 2015 BCSC 1395 at paras 66-67; Byron v British Columbia (Superintendent of Motor Vehicles), 2017 BCSC 1125 at para 81; Cheung v Moorley, 2011 BCSC 1641 at para 77; Alsilmi (Re), 2010 BCSC 282 at para 32-33; Turner v Canada (Attorney General), 2022 FCA 192 at para 9. In Gehl v Canada (Attorney General), 2017 ONCA 319 at para 88, the Court implied the same record would be used in a new hearing when the Court decided that it would be pointless to remit the matter since there was only one possible outcome; and (e) be based on other specific directions of the Court: Shuchuk 2012 at para 42; Dr Mays Abdulghafoor v University of Calgary, 2021 ABQB 187 at paras 121-122; Al-Naami v College of Physicians and Surgeons of Alberta, 2021 ABQB 549 at para 212; Northern Inter-Tribal Health Authority Inc v Yang, 2023 FCA 47 at paras 85-86; Chenjelani v Institute of Chartered Professional Accountants of Saskatchewan, 2022 SKCA 66 at para 55; Chevron Canada Resources v Alberta (Minister of Energy), 1998 ABQB 504 at para 44; Great Canadian Casinos Inc v City of Surrey et al, 2000 BCSC 664 at para 21; Brandt Tractor Ltd v Claypool, 2015 BCSC 759 at para 47; Cheung at para 77; Sunshine Coast Conservation Assn v Sunshine Coast Forest District, 2002 BCSC 145 at para 25. [34] The legislature's ability to limit the Court's remedial powers must be carefully considered in the context of judicial review and its constitutionally enshrined role. See, for example, Dunsmuir v New Brunswick, 2008 SCC 9 at para 31. As pointed out in a different context in Smit v Alberta (Director of SafeRoads), 2023 ABKB 435at para 175, it has long been recognized that “the jurisdiction of the superior courts is not taken away, except by express words or necessary implication”, citing: Albon v Pyke (1842), 4 Man & G 421; Canada (Attorney General) v Telezone Inc, 2010 SCC 62 at paras 42-43.

BOOK_C.title: Additional remedies on judicial review

commentary.text:
This rule gives the court broad powers on judicial review to permit it to craft a remedy appropriate to the circumstances. Ordinarily, having found an administrative decision is unreasonable, the reviewing court should remit the matter for rehearing, unless, “. . . in light of the circumstances and the evidence in the record, only one interpretation or solution is possible, that is, where any other interpretation or solution would be unreason- able”, in which case the court may determine the matter on the merits.
